v.q: What is the difference between `Mono` and `Flux` in Project Reactor?
o: `Mono` emits zero or one item, `Flux` zero to many
`Mono` is synchronous, `Flux` is asynchronous
`Mono` is for numbers, `Flux` is for strings
`Flux` can only emit a fixed number of items
v.w: Both are lazy publishers. Nothing happens until something subscribes.

v.q: Which type represents zero to many items?
o: Flux
Mono
Optional
Future
v.w: Mono is for at most one item and Flux for a stream of items.

v.q: You build a `Flux` pipeline but nothing happens. What is the most likely cause?
o: Nobody has subscribed to it
The pipeline has too many operators
Reactor needs to be restarted
The Flux has been marked read-only
v.w: Reactive streams are lazy. In WebFlux the framework subscribes for you when you return the `Mono` or `Flux` from a handler.

v.q: Which line makes a Flux pipeline actually run?
o: flux.subscribe()
flux.map(f)
flux.filter(p)
Flux.just(1)
v.w: Reactive streams are lazy. Nothing happens until a subscriber requests items.

o: The subscriber tells the publisher how many items it can take
A lock that is held on a single database row until commit
A cache eviction policy that removes the oldest entries first
A way of compressing messages before they cross the network
v.w: Subscribers request items with `request(n)`. Operators such as `onBackpressureBuffer` and `onBackpressureDrop` define what happens when demand is exceeded.

v.q: Which statement about backpressure is NOT true?
o: The publisher decides alone how fast to send
The subscriber requests items
It protects slow consumers
It is part of Reactive Streams
v.w: The subscriber signals demand, so a fast producer cannot flood a slow consumer.

v.q: A WebFlux handler calls a blocking JDBC query on the event loop thread. What is the effect?
o: It blocks one of a few event-loop threads, so throughput can collapse
Nothing happens, because the framework unblocks the call for you
The query runs faster than usual because Netty tunes it
Netty retries the blocked call automatically on another thread
v.w: Use a non-blocking driver (R2DBC) or move blocking work to `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`. BlockHound can detect such calls in tests.

v.q: Which call must NOT run directly on a WebFlux event-loop thread?
o: A blocking JDBC query
A non-blocking WebClient call
A Mono map
A Flux filter
v.w: Blocking one of the few event-loop threads stalls many requests. Move it to a bounded elastic scheduler.

v.q: When is WebFlux a good fit?
o: Many concurrent I/O-bound connections with non-blocking dependencies
Heavy CPU-bound computation that keeps every core busy
Applications that talk to the database only through JDBC and JPA
Small apps whose team only knows how to write blocking code
v.w: Reactive code needs reactive dependencies end to end and a different mindset. For simple blocking stacks, Spring MVC (possibly with virtual threads) is easier.

v.q: Which application is a poor fit for WebFlux?
o: A JPA app with a blocking database driver
A gateway with many connections
A streaming service
An app calling APIs with WebClient
v.w: Blocking dependencies remove the benefit, so Spring MVC is simpler.

v.q: What does `flatMap` do compared with `map` on a `Flux`?
o: `flatMap` turns each item into a publisher and merges them
`flatMap` filters the items while `map` sorts all the items
`flatMap` blocks the thread while `map` never blocks at all
The two operators are identical and can be swapped freely
v.w: Use `flatMap` when the transformation itself is asynchronous, such as a non-blocking call returning a `Mono`.

v.q: Which operator is right when each item starts an async call and the results are merged?
o: flatMap
map
filter
doOnNext
v.w: flatMap subscribes to the inner publisher of every item. map returns a plain value.

v.q: How do Java 21 virtual threads compare with reactive programming?
o: They let blocking-style code scale without reactive operators
They replace the JVM itself with a lighter runtime
They only work when the application is also using Kafka
They move the code from the CPU onto the GPU for speed
v.w: Both address thread-per-request limits. Virtual threads keep simple imperative code, while reactive adds streaming and backpressure semantics.

v.q: Which statement about virtual threads is NOT true?
o: They need reactive operators to scale
They let blocking code scale
They are available in Java 21
They keep the simple thread-per-request style
v.w: The idea is to keep ordinary blocking code and scale it.

v.q: How do you handle an error in a reactive chain?
o: Operators like `onErrorResume`, `onErrorReturn` or `retryWhen`
A `try/catch` around the whole pipeline
Nothing, because Reactor retries by default
Throw the error from `subscribe()` only
v.w: Errors are signals in the stream. A `try/catch` around the assembly code will not see failures that happen later during execution.

v.q: Which operator replaces an error with a fallback value?
o: onErrorReturn
doOnSubscribe
flatMapMany
blockFirst
v.w: onErrorReturn emits a default. onErrorResume switches to another publisher.
